source: 1968 Chevrolet Chassis Service Manual, Engine Electrical, p.6Y-4

procedures.title: Battery electrolyte level: check
steps: Do not overfill; overfilling loses electrolyte and causes poor performance, short life and heavy corrosion.
In service, add only water, never electrolyte.
Never let the level fall below the top of the plates; exposed plate areas can be permanently damaged.
notes: High water usage means overcharging, usually from high battery temperature, a regulator set too high, or a poor regulator ground connection.
Normal water use is about 1 to 2 ounces per month per battery.

procedures.title: Battery top, cables and hold-down: clean and service
steps: Inspect the battery exterior periodically for damage, dirt and corrosion.
With vent plugs tight, wash the top with dilute ammonia or soda solution to neutralize acid, then rinse with clean water.
If posts or cable terminals are corroded, disconnect the cables and clean terminals and clamps separately with soda solution and a wire brush.
Reinstall the clamps and coat them lightly with petroleum jelly to slow corrosion.
Make sure the carrier and hold-down are clean, corrosion-free and sound enough to hold the battery level before installing it.
Tighten the hold-down bolts so the battery cannot shake, without straining the case or cover.
notes: Acid film and dirt on the top can let current leak between terminals and slowly discharge the battery.

procedures.title: Battery charging: safety precautions
steps: Do not smoke near batteries that are charging or were recently charged.
Do not break live circuits at the battery terminals.
Take care when connecting or disconnecting booster leads or fast-charger clamps; poor connections cause arcing.
notes: Charging produces explosive gas that can linger around the battery for several hours; a spark or flame can make the battery explode.

procedures.title: Battery: recharge (slow, fast, emergency boost)
steps: Before any charging method, check and correct the electrolyte level.
Slow charge: charge at about 4 amperes for 24 hours or longer as needed; the battery is full when cells gas freely and 3 corrected specific gravity readings taken an hour apart show no rise.
Fast charge: charge at 40 to 50 amperes for 1-1/2 hours; if electrolyte reaches 125°F first, stop temporarily or lower the rate. Finish with a slow charge to reach full charge.
Emergency boost: charge at 40 to 50 amperes for one-half hour to get enough to crank the engine, then follow with driving or a fast or slow charge.
notes: Only the slow charge brings a battery to full charge.
Do not condemn a battery because it fails to crank after an emergency boost.
